overview: The Republic of South Africa began in 1961 under apartheid, after a referendum that excluded Black people. Pass laws, segregated schools and forced removals shaped daily life, while students, workers, families and artists resisted. A Cape Town hospital team performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967, even as medical access remained unequal. The first national nonracial vote in 1994 brought constitutional democracy, and the 1996 Bill of Rights promised equality, schooling, health care and dignity. Today the country’s many languages and communities thrive amid serious inequalities, including in water and toilets; its history continues.

periods.title: Apartheid republic and resistance
periods.summary: White-minority rule and pass laws continued while students, families and movements organized; Cape Town’s medical team made a landmark transplant.

periods.title: Student uprising and democratic transition
periods.summary: Soweto students protested apartheid schooling; sustained resistance and negotiations led to the first national nonracial election.

periods.title: Constitutional democracy continues
periods.summary: Voters chose a democratic government and a new constitution protected rights. School meals, HIV treatment and access to sanitation are continuing public concerns.

items.text: On 31 May 1961 the Union became a republic after a referendum restricted by race. The imported map begins this record around 1945, but that year did not create the republic. Apartheid had begun under the Union in 1948 and carried on.

Pass books controlled Black South Africans’ movement; residential and public spaces were separated by racial law. Families navigated restrictions on where they could live, work, visit and study. Resistance never disappeared.
In 1976 students in Soweto rose against apartheid education. Their protest is a reminder that children were political actors, not merely people waiting for adults to change the law.

In April 1994 all adult South Africans could vote in a national election regardless of race. Nelson Mandela became the first president of the new democratic government in May. This was a hard-won change in who could shape the country.

The 1996 constitution protects equality and dignity and sets out rights to education, health care, water, housing and children’s protection. A written right is a promise and a tool for change, though it does not instantly deliver a clinic or tap to every home.

South Africa has many home languages. In the 2022 census isiZulu was reported most often at home by 24.4% of people aged at least one, isiXhosa by 16.3% and Afrikaans by 10.6%. A map label cannot tell you what language a family speaks at dinner.

“Nkosi Sikelel’ iAfrika” means “God Bless Africa.” This short original isiXhosa hymn line was written in 1897, sung at anti-apartheid meetings and became part of the combined national anthem in 1997. A few words carry different histories in different voices.

The National School Nutrition Programme gives eligible children a nutritious meal at school. Its guidance includes protein, fruit or vegetables and starch; some schools grow gardens. For a pupil, learning can begin with lunch as well as a lesson.

Apartheid-era forced removals and migrant labour left long family and housing inequalities. The Bill of Rights protects family-linked needs such as housing and children’s care, but families continue to do the daily work of keeping children fed and safe.

At Cape Town’s Groote Schuur Hospital in December 1967, a team carried out the first human-to-human heart transplant. Christiaan Barnard led it, but donor Denise Darvall’s family, recipient Louis Washkansky, nurses, technicians and many specialists were essential. A medical first is a team and family story.

South Africa’s HIV epidemic took many lives. After campaigns for treatment and policy change, public antiretroviral therapy began in 2004. Medicines helped people live longer, while access and prevention remained ongoing work.

The 2022 census found 70.8% of households used a flush toilet nationally. In Limpopo, 57.9% used a pit toilet with or without a ventilation pipe. That is why a question about “the South African toilet” has no single answer: province, income and service access matter.

Under apartheid, public toilets and other amenities were separated by racial law. The democratic constitution rejects that hierarchy, but today’s census shows that unequal sanitation did not vanish with the signs.

ending.text: The Republic of South Africa continues. The 1994 election and 1996 constitution ended white-minority constitutional rule and established democracy; they did not erase the effects of dispossession and apartheid overnight. Its people, languages, schools, arts and public-health work keep changing the country.

sources.title: The Presidency, History of South African Heads of State
sources.note: Union founded 31 May 1910 by negotiation excluding Black South Africans; 31 May 1961 republic followed a racially restricted referendum; 1994 and 1996 constitutional changes.

sources.title: South African Parliament, Diagnostic Report on Social Cohesion
sources.note: 1913 Land Act restricted African landownership and renting to roughly 7% designated reserves; 1936 measure and apartheid removals deepened dispossession.

sources.title: South African History Online, Pass Laws 1800–1994
sources.note: Pass controls preceded 1948; 1952 document law and 1953 Separate Amenities Act restricted Black movement and segregated public facilities.

sources.title: South African History Online, A History of the South African Constitution 1910–1996
sources.note: National Party took power in 1948 and enacted apartheid laws including racial classification, Group Areas and Bantu education.

sources.title: South African Embassy, Chronological Points of Reference
sources.note: 1960 Sharpeville massacre followed anti-pass protest; 1961 republic, 1976 Soweto uprising and 1994 democratic transition.

sources.title: South African Government, Constitution Chapter 1
sources.note: 1996 constitution declares democratic values, citizenship, 11 founding official languages and respect for linguistic diversity.

sources.title: South African Government, Constitution Chapter 2 Bill of Rights
sources.note: Bill of Rights protects equality, dignity, health care, education, water, housing and children’s rights subject to stated provisions.

sources.title: South African Government, Milestones of 20 Years of Freedom
sources.note: 27 April 1994 first national nonracial elections gave adults the vote; Mandela inaugurated 10 May; 1996 constitution followed.

sources.title: South African Embassy, Chronological Points of Reference
sources.note: 16 June 1976 Soweto student uprising against apartheid education; 1980s resistance and 1994 vote.

sources.title: University of Cape Town, World’s First Human Heart Transplant
sources.note: Groote Schuur 3 December 1967 first human-to-human heart transplant required surgeon Barnard, donor family, patient, nurses, technologists and many disciplines.

sources.title: University of Cape Town, First Heart Transplant Team
sources.note: Names physicians, nurses, technicians and other members involved in the 1967 operation.

sources.title: South African Government, HIV/AIDS Milestones
sources.note: Free antiretroviral treatment began in 2004 after an HIV/AIDS crisis and treatment advocacy; South Africa later had a very large treatment programme.

sources.title: Department of Basic Education, National School Nutrition Programme
sources.note: Programme gives eligible pupils a nutritious school meal and encourages school gardens; food supports attendance and concentration.

sources.note: Census figure 8.12: 70.8% households used a flush toilet nationally; 57.9% in Limpopo used pit latrine with or without ventilation. Substantial regional inequality.
